opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the biggest challenges is verification. Language models are remarkably good at generating plausible-looking ideas, code, even entire papers. But plausible isn't the same as correct, and it certainly isn't the same as novel or important. When you let a system run in an open-ended loop, proposing hypotheses, running experiments, writing things up, the bottleneck quickly becomes: how do you know what it produced is actually good?

In some domains you have a clean signal. If you're optimizing a kernel or a loss function, you can run it and measure performance, and that gives you a tight feedback loop, which is where evolutionary approaches combined with LLMs really shine. But the further you move toward open-ended scientific discovery, the fuzzier that signal gets. You end up relying on LLM-based reviewers or judges, and those have their own biases. They can be fooled by confident writing, they can reward things that look like what they've seen before, and they can miss subtle bugs in an experimental pipeline.

The related issue is novelty. These models are trained on the existing literature, so there's a natural pull toward recombining known ideas in incremental ways. Getting them to step off that manifold and propose something genuinely surprising, while still being grounded, is hard. And when they do something surprising, it's often because of an error rather than an insight, so you need a way to tell those apart.

And then there's the human side. If a system generates a thousand candidate solutions, someone still has to trust it, interpret the results, and decide what to build on. So I think the real challenge isn't just generation. It's building the evaluation, the filtering, and the interfaces that let humans and these systems work together, so the automation actually amplifies good science rather than flooding us with mediocre output.

r001.rationale: It says models can readily generate plausible ideas and code, while the central bottleneck is determining whether the output is actually good.

r002.rationale: It discusses approximate evaluation and LLM-based judges, but does not characterize mental simulation of code execution as verification.

r003.rationale: It notes that surprising outputs may result from errors, but does not identify reward hacking or shortcuts as apparent discoveries.

r004.rationale: It calls for evaluation and filtering and mentions measurable feedback in some domains, but does not say discovery problems must be formulated with automatic verification established.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the hardest part isn't getting the model to produce something plausible. It's the specification problem: how do you tell the system what you actually want, and how do you know it got there?

When we build these discovery systems, say an agent that proposes a research idea, writes the code, runs the experiment, and writes up the result, every stage is downstream of some objective we wrote down. And objectives are leaky. If you tell a model "maximize this benchmark number," it will find the benchmark number. It may find it by actually improving the method, or it may find it by quietly leaking the test set, or by picking a weak baseline, or by writing a results section that frames a null result as a win. From the outside, those can look identical. The artifact is a paper, the paper has a table, the table has bold numbers. That's exactly the shape of success, and the shape is what the model is optimizing for.

So the challenge is really about evaluation and verification at scale. A human researcher has years of tacit context: they know which tricks are cheating, they know what a believable result looks like in their subfield, they have a reputation on the line. The model doesn't carry any of that by default. We've had to put a lot of engineering into things like keeping the model from seeing evaluation data, separating the entity that proposes from the entity that judges, and building in explicit reproduction steps. And even then, you're mostly catching the failures you already imagined.

The second layer is that discovery, as opposed to just completing a task, requires taste. Which of a hundred plausible ideas is worth the compute? Humans are honestly not great at this either, but we have at least some sense of the frontier and what would be surprising. Models tend to regress toward the mean of their training distribution. They'll propose the obvious thing, dressed up nicely. Getting genuinely novel directions out of them, rather than well-written recombinations, is still something we don't fully know how to do, and I'd be skeptical of anyone who tells you it's solved.

And then there's a more human issue. If you're having a system discover things on your behalf, you eventually have to trust results you didn't personally derive. That changes the relationship with knowledge. We're going to need new norms, maybe new institutions, for how the scientific community treats machine-generated findings, because the throughput is going to be too high for traditional peer review to keep up. I'd argue that's as much the challenge as any technical piece.

r001.rationale: It says producing something plausible is easier than verifying that the system actually achieved the intended result.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize models’ mental simulation of code execution as a form of approximate verification.

r003.rationale: It describes optimizing a benchmark through test leakage or weak baselines, making apparent success a shortcut rather than a genuine improvement.

r004.rationale: It discusses evaluation and verification, but does not state that formulating the discovery problem must establish how solutions will be automatically verified.

astra-6.text:
I think a major challenge is figuring out what people actually want. If you’re using a language model to search for a solution on someone’s behalf, you need some way to evaluate whether one candidate is better than another. But often the user can’t fully specify that upfront. They might recognize a good solution when they see it, or discover their preferences as they explore different options.

So the challenge isn’t just generating more candidates or making the search more powerful. It’s building a feedback loop where the system can ask useful questions, show alternatives, and refine its understanding of the objective. Otherwise, you can spend a lot of computation optimizing something that’s easy to measure but doesn’t really capture what the person cares about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generating candidates and evaluating preferences, but does not say generating solutions is easier than rigorously verifying them.

r002.rationale: It does not mention language models simulating code execution or characterize such simulation as approximate verification.

r003.rationale: It warns about optimizing an easy-to-measure objective that misses user priorities, but does not identify reward hacking or shortcuts masquerading as genuine solutions.

r004.rationale: It calls for a feedback loop to refine the user's objective, but does not argue that discovery problems need automatic verification of their solutions.

sol-6.1.text: I think a major challenge is figuring out what people actually want. In a lot of discovery tasks, you don’t have a clean reward function or a test that tells you whether a solution is good. People have preferences and constraints that they might not be able to articulate upfront. So the model has to do more than search for solutions—it has to interact with the person, get feedback, and refine its understanding of the problem. Otherwise, you can end up optimizing something that looks impressive but doesn’t really solve their problem.
